Header: 2026-04-22 14:00 UTC — Duration ~45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Singh (Redwood); Maya Patel, Liam O'Connor, Sofia Ruiz (Acme Analytics)
---
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. Busy but excited to get into the SDK topics, we had a few blockers integrating function calls last week.
[00:12] Priya Singh: Cool, yeah we'll go through the snippet and typical gotchas. Quick agenda: SDK usage, function/tool calling, structured output enforcement, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:18] Sofia Ruiz: Sounds great.
[00:23] Liam O'Connor: Just to flag, we ran into some weird parsing when the model returned nested arrays — our parser assumes a flat JSON object.
[00:30] Priya Singh: Yep, that comes up. Two patterns we've seen: 1) use the SDK's schema validation helpers so the model output is validated server-side before you parse, and 2) prefer explicit function signatures so the runtime returns a predictable shape.
[00:43] Jordan Lee: I'll drop the link to the SDK examples in chat — the repo has function call signatures and structured output patterns. (link pasted) https://redwood.ai/docs/sdk (note: auto transcript sometimes shows redwoodai)
[00:51] [00:52] Sofia Ruiz: The link looks good, thanks. A quick question on streaming: if we stream tokens while doing a function call, can we reliably reconstruct the JSON payload if tokens come in partial segments?
[01:04] Priya Singh: Short answer: yes, but you need to use the SDK's streaming helper which buffers until a valid JSON envelope is complete. If you try to parse on every chunk you can end up with malformed JSON because of partial tokens. We also tag chunk boundaries with a sequence id so you can verify ordering.
[01:21] Liam O'Connor: That helps. We also saw the responses sometimes include text before the JSON blob — like 'here's the answer:' then JSON. Any recommendation?
[01:29] Priya Singh: Use the strict schema enforcement flag in the request — it forces the model to return only the JSON structure for that call and the runtime will fail the call if extra natural language is present. In practice we use it for function outputs that must be machine-readable. There's a small risk of model refusing; in that case we fall back to a permissive mode and run a post-parse validation.
[01:47] [02:00] Jordan Lee: On the infra side: a reminder that for the POC you can run on Hosted to iterate quickly, and then we can switch to Dedicated for the latency consistency once you're happy. Maya, you mentioned security reviews — is the team ready to look at Private/VPC options?
[02:13] Maya Patel: Yes we are. We need KMS integration and audit logs, plus SSO/SAML for our users. Also, any notes about data residency? We have EU customers.
[02:24] Priya Singh: We support customer-managed KMS for Private, and we can provide audit logs with per-request metadata including model, route, and tokens. For data residency, you can pin to region-specific Dedicated nodes; for hosted we have EU regions as an option.
[02:39] Sofia Ruiz: Great. On the SDK itself, Liam, can you describe how you're currently calling the function?
[02:46] Liam O'Connor: Sure. We're using the JS SDK to call the /responses endpoint. Our flow: send prompt + tool definitions, expect function call back with arguments. Problem is sometimes the arguments are strings that need parsing into arrays and numbers. We tried auto-parse but it broke on edge cases.
[03:03] Priya Singh: A few tips: 1) declare types in the function signature (array<number> vs string) which helps the runtime coerce types; 2) enable small sampling temperature during function calls so it stays deterministic; 3) if you need strict numerics, consider post-validation and reject if types mismatch.
[03:21] [03:30] Jordan Lee: Also enable the 'kv_prefix_cache' if you have repeated context. It reduces token usage and improves tail latency. Note the transcript sometimes says 'kay-v cache' — same thing.
[03:40] Liam O'Connor: We're looking at KV cache, but our prompt window is often long, so does caching help with mid-sequence calls?
[03:47] Priya Singh: Yes, the KV cache is aware of sequence lengths — it caches prefix layers. For mid-sequence calls it helps if you repeat similar system prompts or static context. We can show a short benchmark.
[03:57] Sofia Ruiz: About error handling: what does Redwood recommend when function calling fails mid-stream? Retry? Backoff?
[04:04] Priya Singh: Retries are safe for idempotent calls. For state-changing operations use the SDK's idempotency keys. For streaming partial failures we surface a 'partial' flag; you can auto-retry from last good offset if operations are idempotent.
[04:18] [04:30] Maya Patel: On monitoring, can we get per-route token and latency breakdown in the Console?
[04:36] Jordan Lee: Absolutely, Console shows token-level cost, per-model latency histograms, and trace links. We'll provide a sample dashboard for the pilot.
[04:45] Priya Singh: Back to structured output: we recommend shipping a JSON schema along with the request. The runtime will validate and attach a validation result block if the output fails; it's safer than ad-hoc parsing.
[04:56] Liam O'Connor: What's the overhead of schema validation on latency?
[05:02] Priya Singh: Minimal — typically <5% added latency for simple schemas. For very complex validation it can be higher. We can run a microbenchmark with your schemas.
[05:12] [05:30] Sofia Ruiz: We also have concerns about hallucinations where the model invents IDs. Any best practice?
[05:36] Priya Singh: Use grounding: provide deterministic sources or tool calls to fetch canonical IDs, and validate against your DB with a post-hook. Function calls that hit your internal services are good — the model returns structured commands and you run the authoritative lookup.
[05:49] Jordan Lee: Quick note on quantization / cost: if you want lower cost we can recommend quantized model variants that still preserve structured output behavior. There's a tradeoff at very low bit widths for numeric fidelity.
[06:02] Liam O'Connor: We'll want a cost/latency chart for hosted vs Dedicated for our typical 120-token responses.
[06:10] Jordan Lee: We'll include that in the pricing doc.
[06:14] [06:30] Maya Patel: For the security deep-dive, do you have standard SOC2 artifacts and a summary of encryption at rest/in transit?
[06:20] Priya Singh: Yes, Jordan will share the SOC2 PDF and a KMS integration doc. For Private deployments we can provide HSM/KMS examples.
[06:30] Sofia Ruiz: Excellent. A small implementation question: our frontend wants to use function calling to open external tools — like a search tool that returns a list of results — what does the pattern look like?
[06:41] Priya Singh: Define the tool schema with explicit fields (query:string, max_results:int). The model returns a function call with arguments and you then execute the external tool and feed results back into the conversation as a new turn. Make sure to enforce timeouts on tool calls.
[06:56] Liam O'Connor: Any caveats for streaming tool outputs back?
[07:01] Priya Singh: Stream tool output as discrete events with sequence ids; the SDK supports event-consuming hooks so your UI can progressively render results. Avoid interleaving multiple tool streams without sequence markers.
[07:13] [07:30] Jordan Lee: Let's confirm next steps: Priya will share code examples and schema samples. Jordan will send pricing and Dedicated pilot SLOs. Liam will run latency tests. Maya will confirm security contacts. We'll meet next week to review results.
[07:45] Maya Patel: Good. One more minor thing — we saw some transcription oddities in the logs, but that's unrelated.
[07:52] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[07:56] Sofia Ruiz: Thanks all.
[08:00] End of meeting
